A Shift operation on a positive integer consists of deleting its first non-zero digit (from left to right) and placing it at its right end. For example, applying three Shift operations to $13025$ gives $5132$. Prove that for all $a,k\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\gcd(a,10)=1$ there exist $k$ pairwise distinct positive integers $n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k$ such that $\gcd(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k)=a$ and any two of them can be obtained from each other by a number of Shifts.

A Triangular operation on trees with $n$ vertices is defined as follows: starting from a tree $T$, we first add an edge so that a cycle of length $3$ is created, and then delete a different edge of that cycle to obtain a new tree. The new tree is the result of a Triangular operation on $T$. Prove that there exists a positive integer $N$ such that for all integers $n>N$ and any two trees $T_1, T_2$ with $n$ vertices, $T_2$ can be obtained from $T_1$ by at most $2n-1405$ Triangular operations.

In a triangle $ABC$, points $D,E,F$ lie on the sides $BC,AC,AB$ such that $$BD=DE=EA\quad\text{and}\quad CD=DF=FA.$$ Let $BE$ and $CF$ meet at $P$. Prove that the orthocenter of triangle $PEF$ lies on $BC$.

Positive reals $a<b$ and a positive integer $n$ are given. First Arash writes a polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients on the board, and then he plays the following game with Babak. In each turn Arash chooses a number $c$ in the interval $(a,b)$ and gives it to Babak. Then Babak chooses one of the $n+1$ coefficients of the polynomial currently on the board, adds $c$ to that coefficient, and replaces the polynomial on the board by the new polynomial. Prove that Babak can play in such a way that, after finitely many moves, the polynomial on the board always has $n$ real roots, regardless of Arash's moves.

Two circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet at the points $A$ and $B$. A fixed point $C$ lies on $\omega_1$, and $P$ is a point varying on the line $AB$, outside the segment $AB$. $R$ and $S$ are the points of tangency of the tangents from $P$ to $\omega_2$, and $Q$ is the second intersection of the line $CP$ with $\omega_1$. Let $O$ be the center of $\omega_2$. Prove that as $P$ varies, the circumcircle of triangle $QRS$ always passes through a fixed point on the line $OC$.

A natural number $n$ is given. Ali is located at a point of the plane in which $n$ points have been colored blue, and he moves according to the following rule; his goal is to escape from the blue points. In each move, Ali chooses an equilateral triangle one of whose vertices is his current position and which has no blue point in its interior, and then moves to an arbitrary point on the perimeter of that triangle. (Points on the perimeter are not considered to be inside the triangle, and Ali's position may coincide with blue points.) We say that he has escaped if he reaches a point with the following property: for every positive real number $C$, he can make a move to a point whose distance from all blue points is at least $C$.

Find the smallest value of $k$, in terms of $n$, such that regardless of the initial placement of the $n$ blue points, Ali can escape in at most $k$ moves.

Given natural numbers $n, k$, Pink Panther and Mr. White play on an $n \times n$ board in turns. Initially all cells are white, and Pink Panther starts. In each turn Pink Panther chooses a row or a column and paints all its cells pink (regardless of whether they were white or pink). In each turn Mr. White chooses $n-1$ consecutive cells in a row or a column and paints them white. If at some stage after Mr. White's turn at least $k$ cells are pink, Pink Panther wins; otherwise the game continues. Find the largest value of $k$, in terms of $n$, for which Pink Panther can be certain to win in a finite number of turns, regardless of Mr. White's play.

A positive integer $N$ and positive reals $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_N$ are given. For indices larger than $N$ we define the sequence $(a_i)_{i=1}^\infty$ inductively as follows: if for $m\ge N$ the numbers $a_1,\ldots,a_m$ are defined, we consider all $\frac{m(m+1)}{2}$ numbers of the form $a_i+a_j$ with $1\le i\le j\le m$ in decreasing order, $t_1\ge t_2\ge\cdots\ge t_{\frac{m(m+1)}{2}}$, and define $a_{m+1}=t_m$. Prove that for every real $c$ there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $a_{n+1}>a_n+c$ for all $n>M$.

For a prime $p>7$ define $$S_p=\{1,2,3,\ldots,p(p-1)\}.$$ Find all functions $f:S_p\to S_p$ such that for every $c\in\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$ there exists $a\in S_p$ with $f(a)\equiv c\pmod{p}$, and for all $m,n\in S_p$ $$(mf(n))^{f(n+(p-1)m)}\equiv f(mn)^n\pmod{p}.$$ Note: the argument of $f$ is always taken modulo $p(p-1)$; for example, if $p=11$, then $f(120)=f(10)$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$, and let $P$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. Points $X$ and $Y$ in the plane are such that $PX\parallel AB$ and $PY\parallel CD$. It is also known that $AC$ bisects $\angle XCD$ and $BD$ bisects $\angle ABY$. Prove that $XY\perp OP$.

For every positive integer $n$ with prime factorization $n=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}\cdots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ (where $p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k$ are its distinct prime divisors and $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots,\alpha_k\in\mathbb{N}$) define $$f(n)=\alpha_1\alpha_2\cdots\alpha_k.$$ Also define $f(-n)=f(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f(1)=f(0)=1$. Find all polynomials $Q\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ for which there exist positive integers $N$ and $a>1$ such that for all integers $n>N$ $$f(a^n+1)\mid f(Q(n)).$$

A function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ and a real number $c$ are given such that $$|f(z)-z|<|z|^{0.99}+c\quad\text{for all } z\in\mathbb{C}.$$ We also know that for any four distinct complex numbers $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4$ whose points in the complex plane are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral (not necessarily in this order), the points $f(\omega_1),f(\omega_2),f(\omega_3),f(\omega_4)$ are also the vertices of a convex quadrilateral (not necessarily in this order). Prove that there exists $a\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $f(z)=z+a$ for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$.
